#### Composing a target instead of naming one

`--
compose-client <id-or-name>` builds an execution stack for this run instead of\nnaming a saved environment, refined by `--compose-
computer`, `--compose-model`,\n`--compose-server-group`, `--compose-skill` and `--compose-secret`. The stack becomes an unnamed,\n
content-addressed environment (the same one `environments ensure-adhoc`\nproduces), so composing the same stack twice reuses one e

nvironment.
`--compose-host` is the deprecated spelling of the same flag.

`--compose-model` and `--compose-secret` carry the d
eployment requirement\ndescribed under [Deployment support for model overrides and secret\ngrants](#deployment-support-for-model-o
verrides-and-secret-grants): a launch that names\n`--environment` / `--client` and `--server` are mutually exclusive: an\nenvironm

ent or client supplies a closed server set that an override cannot
change.

> [!WARNING]
>
> `--refresh-snapshot` **changes t
he suite**, not just this run: it re-derives\n> and stores the suite's host-config snapshot, so every future run uses the new\n> o
ne. It is rejected on any multi-target launch — several runs racing to write\n> one snapshot would leave the suite pinned to which

ever finished last.

#### Output and exit codes

With `--format json`, stdout is **exactly one JSON document** — the launch
r
eceipt, with nothing appended — so CI can parse it directly. In human format\nthe CLI prints a `View:` link per started run, a `St

arted N/M runs (group …)`
summary when several launched, and a `Failed: <target> — <code>: <message>`
line per failure.

With
`--wait`, the default output contains the launch receipt and completed\nruns. `--reporter` replaces that output with the canonical
structured report.\n`--out` writes the same report atomically, including on failed-run and\npost-completion reporting-error paths

, before the command sets its exit code.

Without `--wait`, a partial or wholly failed fan-out **exits 1**; with
`--wait` it ex
its **4** (see the exit-code table above). A per-target failure\ndoes not abort its siblings, so exiting 0 would let a pipeline re

ad "1 of 3
runs never started" as a clean launch.

#### `--file`: upload and run a suite file

`eval run --file` reads the
versioned suite file (`schemaVersion: \"1\"`),\nauthenticates, then validates. A contract-invalid file exits **2** after the\nauth
request — it does not start a run. `eval validate` on the same bytes\nstill exits 1: that command is a verdict on the file; this

one is not.

The file's `suite.id` is the declared suite identity. The first run creates a
file-owned suite stamped with that i
d; later runs of the same id in the same\nproject update that suite rather than creating a second one. A UI-authored\nsuite has no
declared id, so no file can claim it. Resolve is never by name.\n\nFile `passThreshold` is a fraction; the hosted suite grades on
a percent. The\nconversion refuses rather than approximates. A file count above **10**\n(`repetitions` in a `schemaVersion: \"1\"

` file, `iterations` in `"2"`) is
refused by name (`REPETITIONS_CAP`) and is not clamped.

**Which vocabulary the sync speaks
is the deployment's call.** Before writing\nanything, the CLI reads `GET /capabilities` once. A deployment that advertises\n`voca
bulary.version: 2` gets every request with `x-mcpjam-eval-vocabulary: 2`\nand case bodies spelled canonically — `iterations` (the
exact count),\n`legacyIterations` (the legacy floor, the same number) and `assertions` —\ninstead of `repetitions` / `iterations`
/ `checks`. A deployment without the\ncapability block, or without the capabilities route at all, is spoken to in\nvocabulary 1, b
yte-for-byte as before. Nothing in the file changes either way:\nthe dialect of the file and the vocabulary of the wire are indepe

ndent.

Cases are synced in batches of at most 100 (`create_eval_cases`). Every
declared case is created or updated, including
`disabled: true` rows. A case\nthe file **no longer declares** is deleted from the hosted suite before\nlaunch. A case the file st
ill declares but marks `disabled: true` is **kept,\nwith its history** — it is simply left out of the launch, so parking a flaky\n
test does not destroy its past results and re-enabling it later resumes the\nsame case.\nThe run is scoped to the enabled cases ei
ther way. A file with no enabled\ncases is refused (`NO_ENABLED_CASES`) rather than launching the whole\npersisted suite. `--case`
may only name an enabled case. A later run updates\nexisting cases by declared id and creates new ones. An enabled case that\nove
rrides `passThreshold` is refused: hosted grading is suite-wide. A\ndisabled case with the same override is ignored, matching how

repetitions
are checked. Authored
`defaults.toolPolicy` and non-empty `defaults.validity` gates are refused at
hosted CLI launc
h (`TOOL_POLICY_UNSUPPORTED` / the corresponding validity\nrefusal). Hosted platform-authored suites do not currently have a backe
nd\ntool-policy field or enforcement path, so the CLI does not upload a suite that\nwould claim those guarantees. When supported b
y an eval runner, `toolPolicy`\nis enforced at execution time with denied tools kept visible but blocked;\nserver annotations are
advisory and **UNTRUSTED**. The file's default count\n(`defaults.repetitions`, or `defaults.iterations` in `schemaVersion: \"2\"`)
is\ninherited per case and is not uploaded as a suite `minIterations` floor.\nAuthored `defaults.systemPrompt` and `defaults.temp
erature` are uploaded as\nexecution defaults; omitted fields stay omitted so the platform applies its\nown defaults. `target.hosts
` and `target.environment` are attached before\nlaunch. A file environment takes precedence over file hosts for that launch,\nwhil
e an explicit CLI target takes precedence over both. When an explicit CLI\ntarget is provided (for example `--host`), the file's `
target.hosts` are\n**not** synchronized to the suite's persisted host attachments — the suite\nkeeps whatever hosts it already has
. Host attachment synchronization only\nruns when no explicit CLI target overrides the file. Environment attachment\nsynchronizati

on is unaffected and always runs.

Without `--idempotency-key`, the CLI mints a fresh UUID for every invocation
and prints it t
o stderr before launch (`Eval idempotency key: <key>`). Each\ninvocation therefore starts and bills a new run. To retry a launch w
hose\nresponse was lost — without starting a second run — pass the key that was\nprinted: `--idempotency-key <printed-key>`. A rep

lay is marked `deduped` in
the receipt and human output. `--notes` is not part of the key.

##### Imported cases: live tool res

olution, and per-run approval

Every file run performs the same live check `eval validate --project` performs,
**before it writ
es anything**. It is not opt-in and there is no flag to skip\nit. A file with no deterministic `toolCall` steps asks no question a

nd pays no
round trip.

What happens when a deterministic reference does not resolve depends on the
case:

| Case | Outcome
|\n| - | - |\n| Selected (enabled, and named by `--case` if you used it) | The launch **refuses before the suite is synced** — not
hing is written and nothing is billed |\n| Imported, not selected | Its claim is rewritten to `unresolved` (keeping `sourceCaseKey
`) and it is **still persisted**, so the hosted record says what MCPJam found rather than still asserting a claim about a missing
tool |\n| Native, not selected | Left exactly as authored. A hand-written case never acquires an `import` block from this — \"some
body wrote this\" and \"something converted this\" are different facts |\n\nEach target is checked on **its own** server set. `--h
ost` is checked against\nthat host's configured servers rather than the file's, because that is the set\nthe run connects — valida
ting `target.servers` would approve a tool the host\ncannot reach. A host the FILE declares uses its own `servers` list when it\nd
eclares one (those are attached to the host before launch) and the host's\nconfigured set when the field is omitted. An explicitly
empty `servers: []`\nis a real, empty set — it clears the attachment before launch — and is\nvalidated as such, never as an omitt
